title: Branzino al Sale
subtitle: whole sea bass baked in a salt crust
excerpt: Branzino al sale encases a whole sea bass in a thick shell of coarse salt and egg white, then bakes it in a very hot oven. The salt crust seals in moisture and seasons the fish gently from the outside. Serves 2.
sourceNotes: Baking fish in a salt crust is an ancient Mediterranean technique documented across Italian, Greek, Spanish, and North African cuisines. In Italy it is most closely associated with the coastal kitchens of Liguria, Sardinia, and the Amalfi coast, where sea bass (branzino, also called spigola) is the fish most commonly prepared this way. The technique appears in Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), as a method for preserving moisture in whole fish during baking. The egg white in the salt mixture was a later refinement, appearing in 20th-century Italian cookbooks: it binds the salt into a firm crust that holds together when cracked open at the table. The result is a fish that is perfectly seasoned, completely moist, and requires almost no preparation.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The salt crust can be prepared and the fish encased up to 2 hours ahead. Refrigerate until ready to bake.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick shell of coarse salt bound with egg whites that encases a whole fish for baking. The crust does not make the fish salty: the skin protects the flesh, and the salt acts as a heat-equalising shell that retains moisture. The crust is cracked and removed at the table before serving.

content.text: Branzino al sale looks theatrical, tastes simple, and produces a sea bass that is almost impossible to overcook. The thick salt shell keeps the oven's dry heat from reaching the fish directly; what cooks it is a gentle, humid warmth inside the crust. The result is fish that is perfectly moist and finely seasoned but not salty, because the skin acts as a barrier.

The fish needs to be gutted and scaled but left whole with its skin on. Stuffing the cavity with a lemon slice, a few thyme sprigs, or a bay leaf is optional but adds aromatic interest. The crust is cracked open at the table with a spoon or a small hammer, which is part of the appeal of the dish.

items.prepNote: coarse sea salt or kosher salt
sliced, for cavity and to serve
extra virgin, to drizzle on serving

content.text: Heat the oven to 220°C fan (240°C conventional). Mix {{sea-salt-coarse}} of coarse salt with the egg whites from {{eggs}} eggs and {{water}} of cold water. Stir until the salt is evenly moistened: it should clump when pressed between your fingers.

Place a 1 cm layer of salt mixture on a roasting tin slightly larger than the fish. Lay the fish on top. Stuff the cavity with lemon slices, thyme, and bay leaves if using. Cover the fish completely with the remaining salt, pressing firmly to seal. The crust should be about 1 to 2 cm thick all over.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes for a 700 g fish. A digital thermometer inserted through the crust should read 60°C at the thickest part of the flesh. Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes.

with a spoon by tapping firmly along the top. Lift off the crust in large pieces. Peel back the skin and fillet the fish directly from the crust. Drizzle with {{olive-oil}} of extra virgin olive oil and serve with lemon.

items.fix: Add the water gradually and test the mixture: it should hold together when pressed. Add a little more water if needed.

items.cause: Baked for too long, or fish was smaller than expected
items.fix: Calculate 10 minutes per 500 g of fish weight as a rough guide. A digital thermometer gives the most reliable result: 60°C is the target.

items.cause: Skin was not intact, allowing salt to reach the flesh
items.fix: Make sure the fish is well-scaled and the skin is completely intact before encasing. The skin is the salt barrier.

content.text: Branzino al sale is found in coastal restaurants all along the Mediterranean, from Liguria to Sicily to Sardinia. The fish changes by region: branzino in Liguria, orata or spigola in Sicily, whatever the catch includes in Sardinia. The technique is the same everywhere: salt, egg white, oven. It makes an impression when the crust is cracked at the table. It is achievable at home and needs less skill than most fish dishes.
